title: Struct & Interface Embedding
summary: **Embedding** is Go's way of building bigger types out of smaller ones by declaring a field with **no name — just a type**. The embedded type's exported fields and methods are **promoted** to the outer type, so it looks and feels like reuse. But this is **composition, not inheritance**: there is no subclassing and no virtual dispatch, which trips up almost everyone coming from an OOP background.

subtopics.title: Embedding a struct (anonymous field)
subtopics.explanation: Declare a field with only a type and no field name; the type's name (e.g. `Logger`) doubles as the field name, and its exported fields and methods are promoted onto the outer struct so you can call s.Log() directly. This anonymous-field syntax is the entire mechanism behind Go's embedding.

subtopics.title: Method & field promotion
subtopics.explanation: An embedded type's exported methods become callable on the outer type and its exported fields become accessible directly. Crucially, a promoted method still runs with the EMBEDDED value as its receiver — it cannot see the outer struct. Promotion is the payoff of embedding: reuse without any forwarding boilerplate.

subtopics.title: Shadowing & name resolution
subtopics.explanation: A name defined directly on the outer type shadows the same name promoted from an embedded type (shallower wins), and two embedded types with the same promoted name at the same depth is a compile error unless you qualify it (s.Logger.Log()). Shadowing is how you deliberately 'override' a promoted method on the outer type.

subtopics.title: Pointer vs value embedding
subtopics.explanation: Embedding `Logger` copies the inner value into the outer struct; embedding `*Logger` shares one inner value via a pointer, and a nil embedded pointer panics the moment you call a promoted method through it. Choosing value vs pointer embedding controls whether the inner data is copied or shared.

subtopics.title: Interface embedding & wrapping
subtopics.explanation: Interfaces compose by embedding other interfaces (io.ReadWriter = { Reader; Writer }), and a struct can also embed an interface, delegating promoted methods to the stored value — handy for decorators that override just one method. Interface embedding is how Go builds bigger contracts and decorators out of smaller ones.

subtopics.title: Satisfying interfaces via embedding
subtopics.explanation: If you embed a type whose method set already satisfies an interface, the outer type satisfies it too, thanks to promotion — this is how embedding sync.Mutex gives you Lock/Unlock, or how a wrapper reuses a base implementation. Embedding thus lets a type acquire interface satisfaction for free.

subtopics.title: Composition, not inheritance
subtopics.explanation: Embedding looks like inheritance but is composition with auto-forwarding: there is no subclass, no `super`, and no virtual dispatch. A promoted method always runs with the embedded value as its receiver, so overriding a method on the outer type does NOT change the behavior of an inherited method that calls it. Grasping this is the whole point of the topic — it prevents the 'my override is ignored' bug.

foundations.overview: Go deliberately has no classes and no inheritance. Instead it gives you embedding: you put a field with just a type — no name — inside a struct (or list one interface inside another), and the inner type's exported fields and methods are 'promoted' so they appear to belong to the outer type. The result looks like inheritance but works like composition: the outer type HAS-A inner value and forwards to it, rather than IS-A subclass of it.
foundations.formalDefinition: Embedding is the inclusion of an anonymous (unnamed) field in a struct, or of one interface within another. The embedded type's exported fields and methods are promoted into the embedding type's method set and field set, accessible as if declared directly, while the embedded value's own receiver remains the target of its promoted methods.
foundations.whyItMatters: Embedding is how idiomatic Go achieves code reuse and interface composition without inheritance. Understanding that promotion is delegation — not virtual dispatch — is the single most-tested and most-misunderstood point about Go's type system, and it determines whether your 'override' actually does anything.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the outer struct as a manager with an assistant (the embedded value) sitting at the next desk. When someone asks the manager to do a task the manager doesn't handle, the request is silently forwarded to the assistant — who does it from THEIR own desk, with THEIR own tools, never looking back at the manager. That forwarding is promotion; the assistant never sees the manager.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Promotion is resolved entirely at compile time — it is syntactic sugar that rewrites s.Log() into s.Logger.Log(). There is no vtable lookup and no extra cost: a promoted method call compiles to the same code as calling the method on the embedded field directly. The embedded value is stored inline (for value embedding) or as a pointer (for pointer embedding) within the outer struct's memory layout.
foundations.realWorldUsage: The standard library leans on it heavily: io.ReadWriter embeds Reader and Writer; many structs embed sync.Mutex for locking, embed an interface to wrap/decorate it (middleware, instrumented clients), or embed a struct to reuse a base implementation.
foundations.businessImpact: Composition via embedding keeps services flexible: you can wrap a database client, an HTTP handler, or a logger to add metrics or auth without rewriting the original, which shortens delivery time and reduces regression risk.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing that promoted methods don't dispatch back to the outer type prevents a whole class of 'my override is being ignored' bugs and steers engineers toward explicit interfaces and delegation — designs that are easier to test and reason about.
foundations.performanceImpact: Promotion has zero runtime overhead (it's compile-time sugar). Value embedding copies the inner struct into the outer one (larger struct, no indirection); pointer embedding adds one indirection but shares a single inner value and avoids copying large types.
commonUseCases: Embedding sync.Mutex/sync.RWMutex to make a struct lockable
Wrapping/decorating an interface to add logging, metrics, or auth
Reusing a base struct's fields and methods across related types

commonMisconceptions.reality: It's composition with auto-forwarding. There is no subclass, no `super`, and no virtual dispatch — a promoted method's receiver is the EMBEDDED value, not the outer struct, so it never calls the outer type's overrides.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A promoted method can call the outer type's other methods/overrides (polymorphism).
commonMisconceptions.reality: No. A method defined on the embedded type only ever sees its own receiver. If you need the outer behavior, pass an interface explicitly — embedding won't do it for you.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An embedded field and a named field of the same type are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A named field (`log Logger`) is NOT promoted — you must write s.log.Log(). Only an anonymous field (`Logger`) promotes the inner methods and fields.

visualExplorer.title: How a promoted method is resolved
visualExplorer.caption: Calling a method on the outer struct: where the compiler looks, and which receiver actually runs.

config.intro: You call `s.Greet()` on a `Server` that embeds `*Logger`. Here is exactly how Go resolves it:

steps.name: Look on the outer type
steps.detail: The compiler first checks whether `Greet` is declared directly on `Server`. If it is, that one is used and the search stops (shallower wins / shadowing).

steps.name: Search promoted methods
steps.detail: Not found on Server, so it searches the embedded fields at depth 1. It finds `Greet` promoted from the embedded `*Logger`.

steps.name: Check for ambiguity
steps.detail: If two embedded types at the SAME depth both promoted `Greet`, that's a compile error — you'd have to qualify it as `s.Logger.Greet()`.

steps.name: Rewrite the call
steps.detail: `s.Greet()` is rewritten at compile time to `s.Logger.Greet()` — pure syntactic sugar, no vtable, no runtime cost.

steps.name: Bind the inner receiver
steps.detail: `Greet` runs with `s.Logger` (the EMBEDDED value) as its receiver. It cannot see `Server` or any method `Server` overrides — composition, not inheritance.

visualExplorer.title: Interface embedding composes method sets
visualExplorer.caption: io.ReadWriter is literally `interface { Reader; Writer }` — embedding unions the method sets, and any type with both Read and Write satisfies it.

interactiveExamples.title: Promotion: methods and fields come along for free
interactiveExamples.explanation: Server embeds *Logger with no field name. Logger's exported field Prefix and method Log are promoted, so you call them directly on the Server even though they're defined on Logger.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: wrap an interface to override one method
interactiveExamples.explanation: A struct can embed an INTERFACE, delegating every method to the stored value. Here we want to embed Notifier so SMSNotifier inherits Name() automatically but overrides Send(). Fill in the embedding and the override so it prints the SMS line plus the promoted name.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print? (the key is which Describe() the promoted Greet sees)
checkpoints.explanation: Greet is promoted from Animal and runs with the EMBEDDED Animal as its receiver. Inside Greet, a.Describe() calls Animal.Describe() — there is NO virtual dispatch back to Dog.Describe(). This is the heart of 'composition, not inheritance': overriding Describe on Dog does not affect the inherited Greet.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does the standard library write `type ReadWriter interface { Reader; Writer }`?
options: It makes ReadWriter a subclass of Reader and Writer
Interface embedding unions the two method sets, so ReadWriter requires Read AND Write
It copies the implementations of Read and Write
It forces every Reader to also implement Write
checkpoints.explanation: Embedding interfaces composes their method sets. ReadWriter's method set is the union of Reader's and Writer's, so any concrete type that has both Read and Write satisfies it. There are no implementations on an interface — only required method signatures.

checkpoints.prompt: This compiles but panics at runtime. What's wrong?
options: Log isn't promoted from a pointer
s.Log calls a method on a nil *Logger, causing a nil-pointer panic
Server can't embed a pointer type
checkpoints.explanation: Embedding *Logger promotes Log, but s.Logger is nil because we never set it. Calling s.Log("up") is (s.Logger).Log("up") on a nil pointer; accessing l.Prefix dereferences nil and panics. Either embed Logger by value, or initialize the pointer: Server{Logger: &Logger{}, ...}.

checkpoints.prompt: Make Counter thread-safe by embedding a mutex so it promotes Lock/Unlock.
checkpoints.explanation: Embedding sync.Mutex as an anonymous field promotes its Lock and Unlock methods onto Counter, so c.Lock()/c.Unlock() work directly. A named field would require c.mu.Lock(); sync.Once is for one-time init, not mutual exclusion.

codeLab.title: A thread-safe counter via mutex embedding
codeLab.instructions: Implement a `SafeMap` that embeds `sync.Mutex` and stores counts in a map[string]int. Implement `Inc(key)` (increment under lock) and `Get(key)` (read under lock). Then implement `Solve(keys []string) map[string]int` which increments each key once and returns the final counts. Promotion should let you call Lock/Unlock directly on the struct.
hints: Embed sync.Mutex as an anonymous field so m.Lock() and m.Unlock() are promoted onto SafeMap.
Always defer Unlock right after Lock so the lock is released even if the body returns early.
Solve should copy the counts out under the lock before returning, so callers get a plain map.

debuggingLab.title: My override is being ignored
debuggingLab.symptom: A developer 'overrides' Describe() on Manager, but the promoted Introduce() still prints the Employee description as if the override never happened.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Go embedding is composition, not inheritance — there is no virtual dispatch. Introduce is promoted from Employee and runs with the EMBEDDED Employee value as its receiver (e Employee). Inside it, e.Describe() resolves at compile time to Employee.Describe(); the receiver e has type Employee and knows nothing about Manager, so Manager.Describe() is never consulted. The 'override' only applies when you call m.Describe() directly on a Manager.
commonMistakes: Expecting a promoted method to dispatch back to the outer type's overriding method (there is no `super`/virtual call).
Believing embedding creates an is-a subclass relationship rather than has-a delegation.
Assuming defining Describe on Manager changes the behavior of the inherited Introduce.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Restructure so Introduce can call the right Describe. Use an explicit interface and pass it in, so the description is chosen by the caller rather than fixed to Employee's receiver.

theory.question: What is struct embedding in Go, and how is it different from inheritance?
theory.directAnswer: Embedding is declaring a struct field with only a type and no name (an anonymous field). The embedded type's exported fields and methods are promoted onto the outer type, so you can access them as if they were declared directly. It differs from inheritance because it's composition with auto-forwarding: there's no subclass, no `super`, and no virtual dispatch — a promoted method always runs with the embedded value as its receiver and never dispatches back to the outer type's methods.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An anonymous field whose type name acts as the field name, with its exported members promoted into the embedding type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go omits classes and inheritance on purpose; embedding provides reuse and interface composition without the fragility of deep class hierarchies.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler rewrites s.M() into s.Embedded.M() (shallowest match wins). The method then executes with the embedded value bound as its receiver — pure delegation, resolved at compile time.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundation of idiomatic Go reuse and a classic interview trap: candidates who think it's inheritance get the no-virtual-dispatch question wrong.
theory.realWorldExample: A struct embeds sync.Mutex to gain Lock/Unlock, or embeds *log.Logger to gain logging methods, without writing any forwarding code.

followUps.question: Does a promoted method see the outer struct's overriding methods?
followUps.answer: No. Its receiver is the embedded value; it only ever calls methods resolved on that inner type. There is no polymorphism through embedding.

followUps.question: What's the difference between embedding `Logger` and a named field `log Logger`?
followUps.answer: The anonymous `Logger` promotes its methods/fields (s.Log()); the named field does not — you must write s.log.Log().

theory.question: How does Go resolve a method name when multiple embedded types could provide it?
theory.directAnswer: Go uses depth-first, shallowest-wins resolution. A method declared directly on the outer type shadows any promoted one. Among promoted methods, the one at the shallowest embedding depth wins. If two embedded types promote the same name at the SAME depth, the call is ambiguous and is a compile error — you must disambiguate by qualifying it, e.g. s.Logger.Log().

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The name-resolution algorithm for promoted fields and methods.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give predictable behavior when types compose multiple embedded types that may share names.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler searches depth 0 (the outer type) first, then depth 1 (direct embeds), and so on. A unique shallowest match is selected; a tie at the same depth is an error unless explicitly qualified.

theory.whyImportant: Ambiguity errors and accidental shadowing are real-world surprises when composing several embedded types.
theory.realWorldExample: Embedding two structs that both have an ID field forces you to write s.User.ID vs s.Account.ID to disambiguate.

followUps.question: How do you intentionally 'override' a promoted method?
followUps.answer: Declare a method with the same name and signature directly on the outer type; being at depth 0 it shadows the promoted one for calls on the outer type.

followUps.question: Is same-depth ambiguity a runtime or compile-time error?
followUps.answer: Compile time — but only if you actually reference the ambiguous name; otherwise the program still compiles.

theory.question: What is the difference between value embedding (`Logger`) and pointer embedding (`*Logger`), and when would you choose each?
theory.directAnswer: Value embedding stores a copy of the inner struct inline in the outer struct, so the outer type owns its own independent copy and there is no indirection. Pointer embedding stores a pointer, so multiple outer values can share one inner instance and no copy is made — but a nil embedded pointer panics the moment any promoted method dereferences it. Choose value embedding for small structs you want copied together with the outer value; choose pointer embedding for large inner types you don't want to copy, or when the inner value must be shared, and always initialize it in a constructor.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two forms of struct embedding that differ in whether the inner type is stored inline (value) or referenced (pointer).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go needs a way to control copy semantics and sharing of embedded data the same way it does for any other field.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For value embedding the inner struct's bytes live inside the outer struct's memory, so copying the outer copies the inner too. For pointer embedding only the pointer word is stored; promoted method calls dereference it, so a nil pointer causes a runtime nil-pointer panic.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the wrong form causes either accidental copies of large state or nil-pointer panics from uninitialized shared values — both common production bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: A Server embeds *log.Logger so many servers can share one configured logger instance rather than each carrying an independent copy.

followUps.question: Why does a nil embedded pointer compile but panic at runtime?
followUps.answer: Promotion resolves at compile time, so the call is valid syntactically; at runtime the promoted method dereferences the nil pointer to bind its receiver and panics.

followUps.question: Does value embedding a sync.Mutex cause problems?
followUps.answer: Yes if you copy the outer struct after use — copying the embedded mutex duplicates lock state, a data-race bug that go vet flags.

theory.question: How does interface embedding work, and how does embedding an interface inside a struct differ from embedding one interface in another?
theory.directAnswer: Embedding one interface inside another (like io.ReadWriter embedding Reader and Writer) unions their method sets: the composed interface requires every method of each embedded interface, and any concrete type that has all of them satisfies it. Embedding an interface inside a STRUCT is different — it adds a field whose promoted methods delegate to whatever concrete value is stored in that field, letting the struct satisfy the interface for free and letting you override just the methods you care about. The first composes contracts; the second builds decorators via delegation.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two uses of interface embedding: composing method sets between interfaces, and delegating method sets from a struct field.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets Go build larger contracts from small orthogonal interfaces, and build wrappers/decorators without hand-writing forwarding methods.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interface-in-interface produces a method set equal to the union of the embedded sets. Interface-in-struct promotes the interface's methods onto the struct, forwarding each call to the stored value; a method you declare on the struct shadows the promoted one.

theory.whyImportant: It underpins both the standard library's I/O interfaces and the idiomatic decorator pattern, and interviewers probe whether candidates conflate the two.
theory.realWorldExample: A LoggingClient struct embeds an HTTPClient interface, overrides Do to log, and delegates every other method to the wrapped client automatically.

followUps.question: Can you embed an interface in a struct and leave it nil?
followUps.answer: You can, but any promoted method you didn't override will call through the nil interface and panic; store a concrete value to delegate to.

followUps.question: Does embedding a Reader and Writer create a new implementation?
followUps.answer: No — interfaces have no implementations. It only composes the required method signatures into a bigger contract.

scenario.question: You wrap a third-party HTTP client to add request logging, but only want to change one method. How do you do it with embedding, and what's the gotcha?
scenario.directAnswer: Define a wrapper struct that embeds the client's interface (e.g. `type LoggingClient struct { HTTPClient }`). All the interface's methods are promoted and delegate to the stored value, so you only write the one method you want to change — your method shadows the promoted one. The gotcha: if the embedded interface field is nil (no concrete value stored), every promoted method you didn't override will panic with a nil-interface call; and remember promotion is delegation, so your overriding method must call the embedded value explicitly if it still needs the original behavior.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The decorator/wrapper pattern built on interface embedding.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Embedding an interface lets you reuse an entire method set while overriding a subset, without manually forwarding dozens of methods.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Promoted methods forward to the stored interface value; a method you declare on the wrapper shadows the promoted one and can call the embedded value to chain to the original.

scenario.whyImportant: It's the idiomatic way to build middleware/decorators in Go and a common design-round question.
scenario.realWorldExample: An instrumented database client embeds the driver interface and overrides Query to add tracing, delegating the rest unchanged.

followUps.question: How do you call the original method from your override?
followUps.answer: Reference the embedded field explicitly, e.g. c.HTTPClient.Do(req), then add your logging around it.

followUps.question: What if you forget to set the embedded interface value?
followUps.answer: Any promoted method call dereferences a nil interface and panics at runtime — always initialize the embedded value.

scenario.question: A teammate defines a base `Model` struct with a `Validate()` method that other model structs embed, then overrides `Validate()` on `User` and expects a generic `Save(m Model)`-style helper to call the User override. It doesn't. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: This is the classic 'no virtual dispatch' trap. If a method on the embedded Model calls Validate() through its own receiver, it always resolves to Model.Validate() at compile time — overriding Validate() on User never changes what the embedded method sees, because a promoted method runs with the embedded Model value as its receiver and knows nothing about User. The fix is to stop relying on dispatch: define an interface like `type Validator interface { Validate() error }` and have the helper accept the interface value (Save(v Validator)), so the concrete type's own Validate() is chosen at call time via the interface, not via embedding.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A misuse of embedding as if it were subclass polymorphism, where an 'override' is silently ignored by an inherited method.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Embedding is composition with compile-time delegation, not inheritance; Go achieves polymorphism through interfaces, not through the outer type's method table.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Passing the concrete value as a Validator interface stores its dynamic type; calling v.Validate() dispatches on that dynamic type, so User's override runs. Embedding alone would bind the inner Model receiver and skip the override.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the candidate understands the boundary between embedding (delegation) and interfaces (dispatch) — the single most-misunderstood point in Go's type system.
scenario.realWorldExample: An ORM-style layer accepts a Validator interface for each entity instead of embedding a base Model and hoping overrides are seen, so each entity's own validation actually runs.

followUps.question: Could shadowing Validate() on User ever help here?
followUps.answer: Only for direct calls on a User value; a method promoted from Model still calls Model.Validate() because its receiver is the embedded Model.

followUps.question: What's the general rule of thumb?
followUps.answer: Use embedding to reuse behavior, but use interfaces whenever you need the concrete type's behavior selected at call time (polymorphism).

systemDesign.question: Design a middleware/decorator layer for a service's data-store client so you can add tracing, metrics, and caching independently. How would you use embedding, and what pitfalls must the design avoid?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define a small Store interface (e.g. Get, Put, Delete) and build each concern as a decorator struct that embeds the Store interface and overrides only the methods it needs, delegating the rest to the embedded value. You compose them by wrapping: cache(metrics(tracing(base))) — each layer embeds the next inner Store. This keeps concerns orthogonal and lets you add or reorder layers without touching the base implementation. The pitfalls: never leave the embedded interface nil (a promoted, un-overridden method would panic), remember promotion is delegation not dispatch (an overridden method must explicitly call the embedded Store to reach the next layer), and be careful that promoted methods you didn't override still expose the inner behavior unchanged — including any methods you meant to restrict.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered decorator architecture where each layer is a struct embedding the same Store interface and overriding a subset of methods.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Embedding an interface promotes the whole method set so each decorator only writes the methods it changes, avoiding dozens of hand-written forwarding methods per layer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each decorator stores the next Store in its embedded interface field. Overridden methods do their work (start a span, increment a counter, check the cache) and then call the embedded Store to pass control inward; un-overridden methods are promoted straight through to the inner Store.

systemDesign.whyImportant: This is the idiomatic Go way to build composable, testable middleware and a common system-design interview scenario for service clients.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: An instrumented database client wraps the driver: a tracing layer, a Prometheus-metrics layer, and an LRU-cache layer are stacked by embedding, each overriding Query/Get and delegating everything else.

followUps.question: How do you make the layers order-independent to construct?
followUps.answer: Give each a constructor taking an inner Store (e.g. NewCache(inner Store) Store) so you compose them functionally: NewCache(NewMetrics(NewTracing(base))).

followUps.question: How do you keep the design testable?
followUps.answer: Because every layer is just a Store, you can swap in a fake Store at any level and unit-test each decorator in isolation.

followUps.question: What breaks if you forget to delegate in an override?
followUps.answer: The chain stops at that layer — inner layers (and the real store) never run — so an override must call the embedded Store unless it deliberately short-circuits (e.g. a cache hit).

coding.question: Implement a `CountingWriter` that embeds `io.Writer`, counts the total bytes written, and otherwise delegates to the wrapped writer. Provide a Total() method.
coding.thoughtProcess: Embed io.Writer so the wrapper IS an io.Writer (method promotion satisfies the interface). Override Write to record the byte count, then delegate to the embedded writer to do the real work. Keep a counter field and expose it via Total(). Because Write is shadowed, callers using the wrapper get our counting version while the rest of io.Writer (just Write here) is covered.
coding.lineByLine: Embedding io.Writer means CountingWriter satisfies io.Writer via promotion — but we define our own Write, which shadows the promoted one for calls on *CountingWriter. Inside Write we delegate with cw.Writer.Write(p) (the explicit embedded field, since promotion would just be our own method again), add the returned byte count to n, and return the underlying result unchanged. Total() exposes the running tally. Using a pointer receiver is required so the counter mutation is visible.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per Write call (plus the wrapped writer's own cost).

followUps.question: Why call cw.Writer.Write instead of cw.Write?
followUps.answer: cw.Write is our own method — calling it would recurse infinitely. cw.Writer.Write reaches the embedded (wrapped) writer.

followUps.question: Why a pointer receiver?
followUps.answer: The method mutates cw.n; a value receiver would update a copy and lose the count.

coding.question: Build a `SafeCounter` struct that embeds `sync.Mutex` to become lockable via promotion, with `Inc()` and `Value()` methods that are goroutine-safe. Show how embedding gives you Lock/Unlock for free.
coding.thoughtProcess: Embed sync.Mutex as an anonymous field so its Lock and Unlock methods are promoted onto SafeCounter — no forwarding code needed. Keep an unexported int for the count. Inc locks, increments, and unlocks (use defer so the lock releases even on early return). Value locks and reads so it never races with a concurrent Inc. Use pointer receivers because both the mutex and the counter must be mutated in place, and never copy a SafeCounter after use since copying the embedded mutex is a bug.
coding.lineByLine: Embedding sync.Mutex as an anonymous field promotes Lock and Unlock, so c.Lock() and c.Unlock() work directly on SafeCounter without any wrapper methods. Inc acquires the lock, defers Unlock (guaranteeing release even if the body panicked or returned early), then mutates c.n. Value locks the same mutex before reading c.n so a concurrent Inc can't cause a data race. Both methods use pointer receivers because they mutate the mutex's internal state and the counter; a value receiver would copy the mutex, breaking mutual exclusion. The struct must never be copied after first use, which go vet enforces via the noCopy check on sync.Mutex.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per Inc or Value call, ignoring lock contention.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a mutex and a single int field.

followUps.question: Why must the mutex and counter live behind pointer receivers?
followUps.answer: A value receiver copies the SafeCounter, so Lock/Unlock and n++ would act on a throwaway copy, defeating both mutual exclusion and the increment.

followUps.question: What does go vet warn about here?
followUps.answer: It flags copying a SafeCounter after use, because copying the embedded sync.Mutex duplicates lock state and causes races.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Prefer small, focused interfaces and compose them by embedding (io.ReadWriteCloser-style) rather than building deep type hierarchies. Use struct embedding for wrappers/decorators (logging, metrics, auth) so you reuse a base implementation and override only what changes.
productionDeepDive.performance: Promotion is compile-time sugar with zero runtime cost. Choose value embedding for small structs (no indirection) and pointer embedding for large or shared inner values to avoid copies; be aware value embedding increases the outer struct's size.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Embedding sync.Mutex/RWMutex gives a type promoted Lock/Unlock, but keep the mutex unexported in spirit (callers shouldn't lock from outside). Never copy a struct that embeds a sync.Mutex after first use — copying the lock is a classic data-race bug the vet tool flags.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Nil embedded pointers and nil embedded interfaces are silent until a promoted method is called, then panic. Initialize embedded values in constructors and guard against nil at trust boundaries.
productionDeepDive.observability: Decorator-via-embedding is the idiomatic place to add tracing/metrics: embed the dependency's interface, override the hot methods to record spans/counters, and delegate the rest unchanged.
productionDeepDive.security: When wrapping a client by embedding its interface, audit which methods are promoted unchanged — you may be exposing methods you intended to restrict. Shadow or wrap any method that needs an authorization check.

caseStudies.problem: Express combined I/O capabilities without duplicating method declarations.
caseStudies.solution: Compose interfaces by embedding: ReadWriter embeds Reader and Writer; ReadWriteCloser adds Closer.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Composition keeps interfaces tiny and orthogonal, but readers must follow the embedding to see the full method set.
caseStudies.lessons: Small interfaces composed by embedding are more reusable than one large interface.

caseStudies.problem: Add metrics/tracing to a third-party client without rewriting every method.
caseStudies.solution: Embed the client's interface in a wrapper and override only the methods that need instrumentation, delegating the rest.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Less boilerplate than manual forwarding, but a nil embedded value panics and promoted methods bypass your instrumentation.
caseStudies.lessons: Embedding makes decorators cheap, but you must initialize the wrapped value and remember promotion is delegation, not dispatch.

keyTakeaways: Embedding = an anonymous field (just a type, no name); the embedded type's exported fields and methods are promoted onto the outer type.
It is composition, not inheritance: a promoted method runs with the EMBEDDED value as its receiver and never dispatches back to the outer type's overrides — no virtual dispatch, no `super`.
Name resolution is shallowest-wins; a method on the outer type shadows a promoted one, and same-depth ambiguity is a compile error you fix by qualifying (s.Logger.Log()).
Interface embedding composes method sets (io.ReadWriter), and embedding an interface in a struct builds decorators — but a nil embedded pointer or interface panics on the first promoted call.
